claims.claim: Hong Kong should not impose a hard cap on initial SDU rents.
A narrower package of tenure security, an indexed rent band, enforcement investment, and public-housing queue reform is preferable.
First-generation hard rent caps consistently cause supply contraction.
Second-generation controls on rent increases show small or null supply effects.
SDU stock grew from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025 under the 2021 ordinance.
The ordinance's stability reflects a non-binding instrument rather than proof that caps work.
A binding cap removing 10 percent of rent would remove 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years.
A 15 percent cut in initial rents would transfer about 900 dollars monthly to incumbents while pushing 3,000 to 4,000 households per year out of the segment.
A hard cap protects existing tenants at the expense of new arrivals and newly formed households.
Berlin's Mietendeckel caused classified-listing supply to contract within a year.
When Berlin's cap fell, suppressed increases released and new-contract rents jumped above the pre-cap trend.
New York's modest stock contraction stems from its light treatment of first rents.
Tightening first rents would move Hong Kong from the New York model toward the Berlin one.
Inspection covers under 6 percent of SDU stock per year.
A band-based initial-rent cap would require a certifiable tenancy register costing an estimated 40 to 60 staff-years.
Enforcement would systematically miss the most exploited tenants, such as those without written agreements.
No enforcement design was identified that protects the newest-arrival tail first rather than last.
Mr Chan prioritizes a shorter waiting list over rent relief.
An NGO survey of 440 households found 61 percent would trade a rent increase for three-year tenure security and 74 percent for a faster housing offer.
Mrs Wong's account of flats converted to storage contradicts her belief that landlords cannot exit.
The landlords' submission lacks data on actual margins and relies on a survey with a 34 percent response rate.
A hard cap framed as deprivation of income stream would attract compensation claims and judicial review lasting beyond a Council term.
An indexed, reviewable per-square-foot band is defensible as rate-capping rather than confiscation.
The evidence supports tenure security, a light initial-rent band, enforcement investment, and a shorter housing queue.

cites.sentence: **The elasticity evidence cuts against a hard cap.** The working paper's central finding is that first-generation controls—hard caps on rent levels—show consistent supply contraction, while second-generation controls—caps on increases within tenancies—show small or null effects [D6p2].
Hong Kong's 2021 ordinance is second-generation, which explains why stock grew from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025 even as the ordinance operated [D2p1][D6p2].
Hong Kong's 2021 ordinance is second-generation, which explains why stock grew from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025 even as the ordinance operated [D2p1][D6p2].

The same paper estimates that a binding cap removing 10 percent of rent would remove 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1], and models a 15 percent cut in initial rents as transferring about 900 dollars monthly to incumbents while pushing 3,000 to 4,000 households per year out of the segment entirely—mostly new arrivals and newly formed households [D6p4].

The same paper estimates that a binding cap removing 10 percent of rent would remove 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1], and models a 15 percent cut in initial rents as transferring about 900 dollars monthly to incumbents while pushing 3,000 to 4,000 households per year out of the segment entirely—mostly new arrivals and newly formed households [D6p4].
When the Mietendeckel capped rents, classified-listing supply contracted measurably within a year as owners withheld or rerouted flats [D7p1].
When the law fell, suppressed increases released and new-contract rents jumped above the pre-cap trend [D7p2].
The Berlin lesson is explicit: caps bind differently on entrants than incumbents, and the bill is handed to those outside [D7p3].

New York's second-generation scheme shows the same asymmetry from the other direction—stock contraction is modest precisely because the scheme is light at first-rent, the exact point Hong Kong's ordinance left untouched [D8p2].

**Enforcement capacity makes a hard cap largely illusory.** Inspection covers under 6 percent of stock per year, and a band-based initial-rent cap would require a certifiable tenancy register costing an estimated 40 to 60 staff-years to stand up [D10p1].

Worse, the tenants least able to complain are those with no written agreement—like Mrs Wong, who has never received one and reports the ordinance changed nothing she can see [D4p1]—or the newest arrivals.
Enforcement would therefore systematically miss the most exploited tail [D10p2].
The subcommittee could not identify any enforcement design under which the newest-arrival tail is protected first rather than last [D10p3].

**Tenants themselves prioritize differently.** Mr Chan, facing a rent of 5,800 dollars on a third of household income, does not name rent when asked what would help most—he names the waiting list, and says he would accept any rent to leave if the queue were three years instead of five and a half [D3p3].
The NGO survey of 440 households found 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year tenure security and 74 percent for a faster housing offer [D11p1].

Mrs Wong supports a hard cap, but her own account undercuts the exit-fear argument: she reports two flats in her stairwell converted to storage after the ordinance while still believing landlords cannot exit [D4p3]—a contradiction that shows how unreliable anecdotal confidence in landlord behavior is, in either direction.
The landlords' submission deserves skepticism—it concedes no data on actual margins, and its compliance-cost figures rest on a self-reported survey with a 34 percent response rate [D5p3].

But the legal opinion confirms that a hard cap framed as deprivation of income stream would attract compensation claims and judicial review, with a litigation timeline outlasting a Council term [D9p1][D9p3].

But the legal opinion confirms that a hard cap framed as deprivation of income stream would attract compensation claims and judicial review, with a litigation timeline outlasting a Council term [D9p1][D9p3].
The middle instrument—an indexed, reviewable per-square-foot band—is defensible as rate-capping rather than confiscation [D9p2].

It supports tenure security, a light band on initial rents, investment in the register and inspection regime the band requires, and above all a shorter queue—the quantity problem beneath the price symptom [D11p2].
